video_title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
transcript: There’s never been as big a shock  to the semiconductor industry   as the current surge in demand from AI. AI is driving incredible computing demand.  Easily 40-50% above our maximum  capacity, which I’ve never seen before.  Progress in AI has been driven by  exponentially increasing compute.  To sustain that progress, foundries like  Intel will need to manufacture far more   leading-edge compute, both by producing more  chips and by improving what each chip can do.  But the production of these chips is bottlenecked  by tools that Intel buys from their suppliers.  Most famously, ASML’s EUV machines. If they don’t have the equipment,   they can’t make the chips here. I spent two days touring Intel’s fabs to   prepare for these interviews with its leadership. I wanted to understand what it takes to   manufacture the world’s most advanced chips  and how hardware is shaping the future of AI.  I’m joined by Chris Auth, who leads  development of all the processes   that are currently under manufacturing. The thing I want to understand in more   concrete detail is how the development  of a new process actually happens.  If 14A is going to come out in  three years or two years from now,   what is happening from now till then? I want you to walk me through as much   detail as you can, everything from the level  of “how is the yield improving?” to what   kind of telemetry you guys look at? What kind of experiments do you guys run?  I want to understand what is going to happen over  the next two years as concretely as possible.  14A has been in development for  about three-plus years at this stage,   so quite a bit of pre-work has been done to  get it to the stage that it’s at right now.  Right now, we’re getting very close  to where we’re finalizing the process.  We’re finalizing the tool sets  that it will be manufactured on,   and we’re working on the fine-tuning  of each of the process steps.  There are about 2,000 steps in the  factory that you have to go do.  You need to do really intricate work at each  one of those to make sure it’s fine-tuned,   it can go into manufacturing, it can run  thousands of wafers a week on this process,   and it can be repeatable every single time. Right now, you might have a certain yield.  Walk me through how that  increases month over month.  There’s a line running at 14A. What happens from now till next   month that will result in the yield changing? How do you identify where the defects are?  How do you fix that? There’s a constant   process that we go through in identifying defects. There are two main ways that we’ll identify them.  One is we have inline metrology. We have tools that will look at   the wafers and say, “Ah, there’s a defect there,  there’s a defect there, there’s a defect there.”  Then also at the end of line, either electrical  test or we sort and see where the fails are.  We will identify failures, and then we  will get analysis on those failures.  We’ll cross-section it. You were in the TEM lab yesterday,   and you saw how you can get cross-sections. You’ll get a cross-section of a defect,   and from that, you’ll be able to say, “Oh,  that defect is between these layers, so it   must have come from this section of the flow. Oh, we have inline metrology in that section,   which has identified defects. Those are the defects we need to go after.”  What we’ve learned is that you don’t want  to do too much innovation in one node,   because the more innovation that  you do, the more complex it becomes.  While you’ll be able to get that to work, you  need to hit a certain schedule, and that’s the   schedule that your customer ultimately wants. Having that predictable schedule is a key piece.  You’ve got to figure out how much innovation  you can put in in order to meet the customer’s   requirements in the timeline that they need it. Intel learned how costly that tradeoff can   be with delays to its 10 nanometer node,  whose original target launch date was 2016,   but which didn’t begin manufacturing until 2018. Usually Intel has been the keeper of Moore’s Law,   a new cadence of manufacturing  every two years, but their last   set of products slipped almost four years. Intel today having its worst day in four months,   the stock now down more than 15%. I also want to point out Taiwan   Semiconductor up 13% off of Intel’s bad news. Walk me through what lessons you think Intel   has learned from 10 nanometer. Ten nanometer was a good example   of where we had very aggressive targets. We were doing what was called hyperscaling   at the time, so we were scaling much faster  than what had been historically done.  In order to do that, we came up with all sorts  of innovative ideas on how we could achieve that   without new tools, because  the tools weren’t ready.  That put a lot of burden on the process  and a lot of burden on the engineers.  Now, at the end of the day, 10  nanometer is a great technology.  It has world-class yield, it has world-class  performance, it has world-class cost,   but it took us longer to do that  than what we would have liked.  So we’ve tried to take that learning into  future technology nodes and say, “Hey, we   need to limit the amount of innovation we put in  there to make sure that we keep it on schedule.”  What do you think was the main technology that  should’ve been saved for a future version?  EUV was probably the big thing. When we started to define 10 nanometer,   the conclusion was EUV was not ready. EUV is extreme ultraviolet lithography.  It prints chip patterns with light  at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers,   about 14 times shorter than that emitted by  previous tools that chipmakers had relied on.  The shorter the wavelength, the finer the  features that a single exposure can print.  But Intel decided this technology  wasn’t going to be ready in time.  TSMC transitioned to EUV much sooner.  It put EUV into volume manufacturing in 2019 and  ramped it up further on its 5nm node in 2020.  Intel’s first EUV process did not reach products  until 2023, so TSMC had about four more years   of experience with these machines. Yesterday, we were at the research   lab getting a preview of 2D materials  and CFET and ruthenium interconnects.  I’m curious about how you decide whether that  technology is mature enough for the next node.  One thing that did also come out of 10 nanometer  is we started to define a set of maturity metrics.  We use those maturity metrics in a process  which we call phase gate, where we would say,   “To go from pathfinding into development,  these are the criteria that we need to go hit.”  There are yield criteria, defect criteria,  performance criteria, and we need to hit those   in order to move to the next set of the flow. If there’s something that doesn’t make that,   then it misses that, and it  goes on to the next technology.  We focus on the items that are ready and  we can run and put into a process, because   one of the key things is staying on schedule. Staying on schedule is hard partly because new   transistor designs take decades to mature. Modern chip transistors evolved from the   planar MOS transistor, demonstrated in 1960. The history of transistors since has been   the progression from two dimensions into three. Each development that Chris goes on to describe,   from FinFET to gate-all-around,  is a step in that progression.  So it’ll help to first look at a basic transistor  and how its parts have changed over time.  A transistor is basically a switch. When it’s turned on, it allows current   to flow between its two ends, which  are called the source and the drain.  A piece called a gate sits on top of the  silicon between the source and the drain.  Applying a positive voltage to the gate  turns the switch on, because the positive   voltage pulls negatively charged electrons  in the silicon beneath up toward the gate.  However, a thin layer of insulation stops  them from actually reaching the gate.  So the electrons collect just beneath that  insulation and form a thin conducting path   from the source to the drain. This is called the channel.  Remove the voltage and the electrons disperse,  the channel disappears, and the switch turns off.  As transistors shrank, the source  and the drain got so close together   that current could flow through the channel  even when the switch was supposed to be off.  We needed a better way to control the channel  and prevent current from leaking through.  The fix was to give the gate a tighter grip  on the channel by touching it from more sides.  In the original planar transistor, the  gate only touches the channel from the top.  The FinFET transistor squeezes the channel  into a thin vertical fin of silicon.  The gate drapes over the fin, so it  controls the channel from three sides.  The next progression from there  was to cover not only the top and   the sides of the channel, but also the bottom. This technology is called gate-all-around, and   it slices the channel into thin ribbons, each of  which gets completely wrapped around by the gate.  But getting gate-all-around to work required  new materials and new manufacturing steps.  To build these floating ribbons of silicon,  you first sandwich them between alternating   layers of a temporary placeholder material, which  holds the space where the gate will eventually go.  We use a placeholder because the materials in  the real gate wouldn’t survive the processing   that comes after, which involves baking  the wafer at around 1,000 degrees Celsius.  Once these hot steps are  done, chipmakers etch away the   placeholder, leaving the ribbons suspended. Then they fill the gaps around every ribbon   with a thin coat of a special insulator called a  high-k material, whose purpose is to let the gate   pull more strongly on the channel. And then on top of this material,   they put the metal of the gate itself. FinFET was demonstrated in a lab in 1989   and reached volume production at Intel in 2011. A gate-all-around transistor had been demonstrated   a year earlier, in 1988, but Samsung didn’t  begin producing gate-all-around chips until 2022.  So these ideas, FinFET and gate-all-around,  were developed around the same time,   but they reached production a decade apart. I wanted to ask Chris why it took so long to   get to this current gate-all-around technology. Maybe you can walk me through the process of   getting into high-volume manufacturing. I want to understand concretely,   once you have an idea that, “Hey, we’re going  to make the channel smaller, we’re going to   surround it…” All the other problems of material  science, figuring out how to not destroy the gate,   how do they actually get figured out? Why does it take so long?  Gate-all-around’s a good example, because  back in the ’90s we knew of this idea.  But we knew there were going to be  these problems on how you put this   into high-volume manufacturing. At the same time, there are other   things like high-K metal gate. There’s strained silicon,   there’s FinFETs that are out there. It’s a question of when’s the right   time to go and tackle those? Well, you don’t want to   tackle something before you have to. If you have these other things that can drive   performance, you would go and do that. So we went through this path.  We did strained silicon, high-K metal gate,  we did FinFETs, and then it became, “Well,   we need to do things further. How do we get there?”  Well, gate-all-around’s really  the ultimate transistor out there.  Maybe it’s time to go and start tackling  some of those issues that you have.  You’re right, now you have to look at how do you  put high-K metal gate in with gate-all-around.  It’s that innovation that takes time. Sometimes you need new materials.  Sometimes you need a different tool  in order to be able to do some of the   things that you need to go do, and that  requires invention from the tool vendors.  You have to go to the tool vendor and  say, “Hey, I need a tool that can do XYZ.  I need a gas that can deposit this  particular material that goes into that.  I need a heating chuck that  has this characteristic to it.”  All those things take time. Some of it’s iterative,   where you have to run a gate-all-around  transistor and say, “Oh, well, that didn’t work.  Let me figure out what was  wrong with my hypothesis and   try it again with some different structure.” How has the nature of R&D changed from the era of   just making planar transistors smaller and smaller  and getting the benefits of Dennard scaling,   to the world we’re in today? Is it just a totally different   kind of R&D process? Previously it was,   “Let’s make things smaller, smaller, smaller.” Now you look at all these other facets   of performance at the same time, and  improvements in size don’t come as easily.  Walk me through whether there was some crucial  change in the R&D process at that point.  If you look at the ’80s and ’90s, yes, it was  driven really by Dennard scaling, lithography.  We just made things smaller, transistors  got faster, they got more reliable,   and it was a very predictable cadence. When we started to hit the 2000s, we saw,   “That’s not good enough anymore. We need to do something different.”  To me, it became this golden age of innovation. For each technology node,   how are you going to provide more scaling? How are you going to provide more performance?  It drove things like strained silicon. It drove high-K metal gate.  It drove FinFETs. It drove gate-all-around. It drove backside power.  These are things that in the ’80s  and ’90s you would be like, “Oh no,   we’re not touching any of that,” because we  just continued to have the same process flow.  We just scaled it, scaled it, scaled it. But for somebody like me who’s a   transistor junkie, it’s awesome,  because now the playbook’s open.  You can do all sorts of things out there. You can bring in new materials.  Just look at the number of materials we used  to use in the ’90s versus the materials today.  It’s probably gone up 10X. There’s a lot of innovation.  There’s atomic layer deposition. You’re controlling this stuff atom by atom.  So it’s changed a lot how  you approach the process.  Before, it was, “Try to not change anything.” Now it’s, “Take the sledgehammer and start tearing   the thing up and come up with some new idea.” For 14A, Intel is using a new kind   of lithography machine: High-NA EUV. It uses the same extreme ultraviolet light   as today’s EUV machines, but changes the optics. NA, or numerical aperture, is a measure of how   wide a cone of light the machine’s  mirrors can focus onto the wafer.  The wider the cone you can focus, the  smaller the spot that your light can carve.  Standard EUV machines have an NA of 0.33. High-NA widens it to 0.55.  So High-NA can print features about  1.7 times smaller in a single pass.  When features are smaller than the lithography  machine can print, chipmakers have to split   the pattern across several passes, each  printing a different set of features.  The most tightly packed patterns can  require two, three, or even four passes.  Each additional pass takes up valuable time  on a machine that costs around $200 million,   and it introduces another opportunity for defects. High-NA machines cost about twice as much,   but they can reduce the number  of passes that are needed.  So the question which determines  whether they justify their higher   price is how much more time they save and  how much they reduce the risk of defects.  Now you guys are using High-NA EUV  tools for 14A, whereas TSMC has said   that they don’t make economic sense yet for them. How do you decide whether the next litho tool is   the one that is ready to adopt or not? High-NA’s a good example of where,   because of the architecture of our technology  versus TSMC’s, we make different conclusions   off of the same tool set. We use backside power.  That means that you actually alleviate some of  the pitch requirements you have on the front side.  That allows you to print  that directly with High-NA.  TSMC has to run tighter pitches  because they don’t have backside power,   and they can’t do that with High-NA, so  they have to use double patterning EUV.  So for them, it’s not very helpful. For us, it is very helpful.  Now at 14A, we’ve left it as an option, and  it’s something that we’ll have a discussion   with the customer on, because there’s some  value proposition to it, and there’s some   complexity that it adds. Chris is referring to   a feature called backside power. A chip has two different kinds of wiring.  Power lines deliver electricity to the  transistors, and they need to be thick.  Signal lines let the  transistors talk to each other.  They’re much thinner, but they need to be spaced  apart so that the signal from one wire doesn’t   interfere with the signal from another. In the past, all of these power lines   and signal lines had to be crammed  together on top of the transistors.  Intel’s newest process moves these power lines  below the transistors, to the back of the wafer.  This frees up space on top, so the signal  lines don’t have to be packed as tightly.  This change makes High-NA worth it for Intel. Without backside power, the wiring is so   tight that it would require multiple  passes to print, even with High-NA.  With backside power, a single  High-NA pass is enough.  Outside companies can now commission Intel  to manufacture chips that they’ve designed.  They follow Intel’s process design kit, or PDK:  the menu of what a given process can build,   and the rules for building it. Do you need to lock that into   your PDK right now for customers who  are planning on developing on 14A?  It’s an option in the PDK today, and we’re  handling it as a customer-by-customer   discussion as to whether or not they  want to go down that path or not.  For 18A, there was public reporting that  there were delays in or issues with the PDK,   such that some instructions didn’t work,  and it was difficult for people to use   your foundry to build their chips. Tell me about the process of Intel   becoming a foundry and then having a  PDK that other customers can use to make   whatever chip they’re making as well. There’s definitely a learning curve to   how you become a foundry. That’s something that our   competitors have gone through as well. PDK is a good example of that.  For decades, we’ve been an IDM. We’ve gone to our product teams   and shown them our transistor data, and we  share that data back and forth, and we haven’t   had a formal PDK-type process. So that’s a new process that   we’ve had to implement on 18A. 18A started out not having a PDK.  There’s definitely a lot of feedback we’ve  gotten from the customers as to what they expect   for quality and maturity of the PDK and what  sort of information they want to see in there.  We’ve tried to incorporate that into  making sure that we have a PDK that   meets our customers’ requirements. That’s where we’ve ended up.  We’re starting to get PDKs that have this,  and 14A will have that from the get-go.  It has very high quality PDKs. Again, there are maturity metrics for   what is a PDK 0.5 versus a 0.9 versus a 1.0. We’re constantly going through and taking   customer feedback and incorporating  that into the quality of our PDK.  For most of its history, Intel’s  fabs made only Intel’s chips.  That could be part of what  allowed TSMC to gain an edge.  Serving many customers gave TSMC more wafers  to learn from, more revenue to reinvest,   and more pressure to hit deadlines. Basically, all enterprise customers   have a shared set of product requirements  that you have to meet if you want to even   start talking about doing business with them. These are things like SSO, so employees can   log into your app with their company accounts, or  directory sync, so that whenever someone leaves,   their access gets shut off automatically. These features are harder to get right than   you think, and the risk-reward for building  them in-house doesn’t really make sense:   a slightly better version of SSO  probably won’t accelerate your growth,   but a broken one will definitely stunt it. WorkOS gives you access to battle-tested versions   of all the most common enterprise features—things  like SSO, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs, and more.  WorkOS also has versions of these features that  are purpose-built for agents, so they can log in,   grab the right permissions, and  take actions within your product.  All of these features can be plugged in  with just a few lines of code, so you can   add them and get started selling to enterprises. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Thinking Machines—as well   as more than 3,000 other companies—all rely on  WorkOS to meet their enterprise requirements.  If you want to join them, go to  workos.com and tell them that I sent you.  If a butterfly flapped its wings in the ’60s,  could you imagine a world where gate-all-around   is not even a word people have heard of, an idea  people are familiar with, but people are thinking   of an extremely different branch of the tech tree? How far down the tech tree do you think   things could be totally different? Could it be that we’re not even using copper?  If you look at, say, transistors and  interconnects, where we’ve gotten to,   as far as the transistor and gate-all-around  and it being the ideal transistor structure,   was somewhat inevitable. As I said, in the ’90s we were   already talking about these types of things. Backside power, that one’s pretty out there.  Even in the ’90s, the idea that you’re going to  strip off the entire silicon substrate and put   lines on the backside, that one is probably  something that’s a little bit out there.  Copper, of course copper wires are the  best, so I don’t know how you would end   up somewhere else besides copper. But you guys are exploring other—  For some of the very tightest pitches, it’s  inevitable that you will replace copper.  That’s a good example of where you will have  another material that will come in there.  But for the larger lines, I think  copper is about where it’s at.  Once you start to do gate-all-around  transistors and you do backside power,   now you start to enter a very different regime.  Now you see it’s not, “Hey, there’s just some  substrate and you stack everything on top.”  Now you’ve got a transistor which is floating  in interconnect, and you’re like, “Okay, well,   why don’t I have transistors, interconnect, a  little more transistors, more interconnect?”  This whole 3D stacking that we now do with just  discrete chips that we stack on top of each other.  Now you’re like, “Why can’t I just  build an entire structure like this?”  You see it with memory, NAND, DRAM. They have some incredible 3D structures.  NAND already does it, DRAM talks about  it, but I think that DRAM inevitably   is going to go there too. A lot of people say, “Oh no,   we’re not going to do this because we  can’t do it in the next five years.”  Well, come on, let’s put a  larger timescale on this.  Let’s put 10 years, 20 years. In 2045, do you think you could do it?  Now you start to say, “Oh yeah,  I could see us having some pretty   exotic structures at that point.” We limit ourselves by what we see   as possible in the next four years. As I’ve always said, when people say,   “How do you see technology scaling going?”,  we have visibility for about four years.  Then you get out to the four years, and  you go, “Yeah, I think there’s something   we can do another four years out of that.” And you get to that four years, and you’re like,   “Yeah, I think you can do something.” But if you start to talk about 10 years,   it becomes hard to say what it’s going to be. Chris’s idea of building upward could start   with the transistors themselves. Chips use two types of transistor,   called n-type and p-type, which work the  same way, but with the charges reversed.  Nearly every circuit is built by pairing them up. Today, chipmakers build them side by side.  The next step is to stack them directly on  top of each other in order to save space.  In principle, that fits twice as  many transistors into the same area.  This design is called a CFET, short for  complementary field-effect transistor.  But every extra layer adds manufacturing steps  and cost, and also leads to heat building   up that doesn’t have a clear way to escape. Because logic consumes more power than memory, you   can’t do stacks of DRAM that make HBM or 3D NAND  as easily with logic, because of the heat issue.  Is that the fundamental issue over the long run? How you—  Thermals. There are three things you have when  you try to say, “Hey, what limits compute?”  It’s how fast can you do the switch,  so the frequency of the device.  How much power does it take in order to do  that switch, so the power efficiency of it.  The third one is, how do you dissipate the  heat that was generated by doing that switch?  That’s the thermals piece of it. These are not new problems.  You can go back 20 years and you can  see articles on these three things.  The question is, thermals… how do you  deal with that, particularly when you   start to talk about these 3D-type devices? There is a need for that sort of system-level   analysis and simulation tools. I think we’re in its infancy   because we’ve just started to look at this. It is a limiter, and it will be a limiter, but   again, these are problems that we can go solve. The problems respond to work, but engineering time   is finite, and so are the wafers for experiments. Deciding where they go across thousands   of problems is itself one of the  hardest parts of bringing up a node.  I sat in on one of Intel’s Hot Topics  meetings, where those decisions get made.  I’m here with Kevin Fischer, who was laying down  the law this morning at the Hot Topics meeting,   where you guys were discussing how you’re  improving 18A and 18A-P technologies.  People would come to you with different  experiments they were running,   different ideas they had for improving  yield and performance, and then you and   your integration engineers would tell them  what data you needed, how they should proceed,   how you think they could move things faster. I want people to have a sense of   the culture at these meetings. One thing I found striking is that this   is bottlenecking your most advanced node. You want progress to happen fast,   so you kind of lay down the hammer. I would say the average engineer doesn’t   understand the stakes or the urgency of how  this is going to impact Intel’s bottom line,   how it’s going to impact our customer. They just have no visibility into those issues.  They will typically have a certain set  of criteria that they want to go capture.  They’ll hit boundaries of, “I asked for  something and someone said no, and I’m done.  I guess I can’t have this thing that I asked for.” One thing you learn in this industry is that   you will never have a complete data set. If you want to wait for a complete data set,   you’ve waited too long. It’s already too late.  A lot of what I end up doing in those  meetings is deciding how much risk we’re   going to take on a certain decision  or not take on a certain decision.  You need to say, “Look, do we go now? Do we start risking production?”  Because you’re risking the bottom line. You’re risking revenue.  I’m worried you’re going to put me in  the light of being an ogre because I’m   putting the hammer down on people. That’s a great reputation to have.  It’s really conveying urgency. Every day counts.  Can you walk me through a  particular issue that might come up?  One of the examples you saw  this morning is epi nodules.  Epi is short for epitaxy, which means growing  new material on top of an existing one.  Chipmakers flow gases over a heated wafer,  and the gases leave atoms on its surface.  The crystal structure of the material  underneath acts as a template.  Each new atom lines up with the atoms below it,  and the new layer continues the same crystal.  Chipmakers use epitaxy at  several stages of making a chip.  In the step Kevin describes, they use it  to grow the source and the drain as small   crystals on either side of the gate. During the deposition of our epitaxy,   we get abnormal growth, a  little thing like a tumor.  It’s growing super fast. That causes problems,   because one epi will short to the wrong  epi and you get transistors not working.  Then you’ve got to narrow it down  to how you’re going to fix it.  For the past decade, Intel’s chips have  had this feature called Processor Trace.  When you turn it on, it starts recording all  the code your program runs, and it captures   enough detail that you can go back later  and reconstruct every single function call.  Most companies don’t need that level of detail. But Jane Street does: they need to investigate   specific, fleeting moments in  their trading systems—things like   a delayed response to a network packet. Those events tend to be too brief for   most debugging tools to catch. So when one of Jane Street’s   engineers noticed Processor Trace,  he started playing around with it.  And then he and a summer intern turned that  exploration into a new tool called magic-trace.  Magic-trace leverages the output from  Processor Trace to give Jane Street a   history of every function call leading  up to a specific moment of interest.  This project was completely bottom-up—it  started just as something that one   engineer thought would be valuable. And now, traders and developers across   Jane Street use magic-trace every single day. If you want to work somewhere where you’re trusted   to pursue the ideas that you think matter most,  Jane Street is hiring researchers and engineers.  Go to janestreet.com/dwarkesh to learn more. One of the pieces that you observed this morning   was a special clean that we were looking  at, which would eliminate the nodule.  The nodule would deposit,  and then we’d get rid of it.  Some of the other discussion was  about the source of the nodule.  Get rid of the source of the nodule. There’s some issue. How do you   decide what the source of it is? For the most part, we work highly parallel.  How do you decide? It’s not always evident   what the easiest way to fix the problem  is, so you work on all the potential fixes.  Sometimes it’s not the one you expect first. Once we’ve identified it as a primary problem   for the technology, that’s where this  Hot Topics meeting gets involved.  That’s how we align the resources  into those engineering teams so that   we can accelerate the work. You said that there’s some   fast-track process where wafers can move through  faster if they’re bottlenecking some experiment.  We have a tiered system of what  we call hot boxes in the factory.  Every grade of hot box goes a little bit faster. It’s just how the factory prioritizes that   particular lot, that block of silicon  that’s running through the factory.  Our highest grade of hot box,  HotBox 1, races through the factory.  It gets priority at every single tool,  but it’s a drag on the entire factory.  If you had a factory person in here,  they don’t like playing that card,   because you end up using the tools  inefficiently so that you can go super fast.  Think of it as a highway, and you set  aside that one lane for the carpool,   which everyone could use, but you’re  saying, “Okay, it’s just the carpool.”  That’s our HotBox 1. Everyone clear out of   that lane except for that one experiment, and  that one experiment races down the highway.  Kevin’s job is deciding what goes onto the  production line now, but the day before, I   went to Intel’s research lab with Jack Kavalieros  to see ideas that aren’t ready for the node yet.  We started with wiring. A transistor is only useful once it’s connected   to others, and on a modern chip that takes  more than a dozen layers of metal wire stacked   above the transistors, called interconnect. Those wires are made of copper, and as they   shrink, copper starts to run into trouble. Imagine two chips side by side,  communicating through their facing edges.

but only twice the edge length for connections. This is the area-versus-perimeter problem.
As transistors become denser, a chip’s  ability to do computations increases
faster than its ability to move data around. The industry has known about this problem
for years, so multiple technologies  have been invented to address it.
The completed circuits must undergo two  last operations: bonding and packaging.
Once a chip is made, it still has to be connected  to other chips and to the rest of the computer.
That step is called packaging, and it has  changed a lot in the last few decades.
At a high level, you can think of the  evolution of packaging like this: initially,
chips were laid out side by side. Wires connecting them went out
the side of one chip to another. To allow for more communication
density, the industry introduced a  shared piece of silicon, called an
interposer, for multiple chips to sit on. A chip can talk to other chips through the
wiring that runs directly through the interposer. This type of packaging is often called “2.5D”.
Another way to increase connection density  is to bond chips directly to one another.
This allows for shorter connections between chips,  but the early versions of this idea used solder
bumps, which are bulky and increased resistance. It would be better to skip the solder and fuse
the signal wire connections of the  two chips directly to each other.
This is called hybrid bonding, and  it is one of the technologies the
semiconductor industry is investing in the most. Hybrid bonding works by aligning the copper
interconnects of one chip with those of another. Then these chips are pushed together and heated
so their interconnects expand and  bridge the gap between the chips.
This process makes the insulating  surfaces around the copper bond as well.
And so by removing the solder bumps,  you end up with much denser connections.
But the reason this technology is only now  entering volume manufacturing is because
it took a while to iron out the alignment  and defect challenges that it introduced.
